name: North Face (Kloke-Tindall Route)
approach: Via the Cascade Pass Trail and Cache Col to a high camp near Kool-Aid Lake/Cache Col, then across to Art's Knoll — the saddle directly across the valley from Spider Mountain — which gives access to and a view of the north face and its bergschrund before committing to the climb.
descent: Most parties reverse the same north-face snow/ice line back down to the bergschrund and Middle Cascade Glacier; parties continuing the Ptarmigan Traverse may instead exit via the southeast gully/east ridge to Spider-Formidable Col.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: About one mile and 700 ft below Cache Col on a boot path. The usual first camp south of Cascade Pass and the base for Spider, Formidable and the south side of Magic.
bivy.water: The lake and snowmelt
bivy.permit: No permit required; the lake is outside the national park
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites on rock and heather benches around the lake

bivy.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
bivy.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
bivy.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
bivy.permit: This is the last ground on the park side, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

bivy.name: Spider-Formidable Col
bivy.notes: The working base camp for both Spider Mountain and Mount Formidable, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
bivy.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

previousAttempt.notes: Both opened reports are two-day trips, but camps varied: a hollow ~500 ft below Cache Col (Dec 2011) and Art's Knoll itself (Mar 2013); Kool-Aid Lake is used as the row's main camp. Schedule times come from the Dec 2011 report. Row gain_ft and dist_km are null; day mileage and gain are rough estimates from row waypoint elevations and are not sourced, so treat them as approximate. Winter road closures added ~4 mi each way in both reports (not included).

name: West Ridge / West Face (via Boiling Lake)
approach: Reached from the same Crater Creek/Eagle Lakes Trailhead system, branching toward the Boiling Lake basin rather than continuing to Cooney Lake.
descent: Reverse the west face/west ridge scramble back to the contour bench and Boiling Lake basin; no rappels reported.

previousAttempt.reason: Opened trip reports (climberkyle 2016, Yellowleaf 2017) climb Switchback by the southeast ridge from Cooney Lake; the only description of the west ridge/west face from Boiling Lake is a Mountaineers route page that could not be opened. Too thin to write an itinerary for this specific line.

name: Southeast Spur (East Peak)
approach: Start at the Mirror Lake trailhead at the end of Forest Road 5480 (about 3,600 ft). Hike the Mirror Lake trail to the lake, mostly level, then follow the PCT to the lake's south end and find the boot path.

previousAttempt.notes: Gain is derived from the row's 3,600 ft trailhead to the 5,395 ft East Tinkham summit. Miles is approximate from the Mirror Lake distance (~1.2 mi each way per the Mountaineers/WTA Mirror Lake figures) plus the boot path. SummitPost log entries describe the SE route as an easy, well-worn boot path. No source times this route on its own, so hours is an estimate.

name: West Slope - East Arete (Original Route)
approach: Same general Southern Pickets approach as the South Route — via Goodell Creek, The Barrier, and Crescent Creek Basin — continuing to the notch/saddle between Himmelhorn and West Twin Needle rather than climbing directly from the basin.
descent: Downclimb the class 2 west slope back to the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the separate Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is legally awkward: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is not on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is walk-up only — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

previousAttempt.notes: Abegg's 2009 Twin Needles trip (Thread of Ice, a different line) was 3 days: approach to Crescent Creek Basin, a climb day ending on West Twin Needle (Class 3-4, ~5.6 crux below the west summit), and about 5 h back to the car. Her Pickets page supplies the approach elevations (cairn ~1,800, Terror Creek ~2,100, Stump Hollow ~5,600, saddle ~6,400). The AAC note only says the West Needle is easy from the notch area; I found no description of this route's 'West Slope - East Arete' line beyond that. Day gain is derived from the row's waypoints (500 ft roadhead, 6,050 ft basin camp, 7,936 ft summit). Miles and summit-day hours are estimates.

name: North Face
approach: The standard access to Golden Horn's north side starts from the Rainy Pass PCT North trailhead on Hwy 20, following the PCT north over Cutthroat and Granite Passes and up the small, unsigned spur to Snowy Lakes (~6,700 ft); a rougher, off-trail alternative bushwhacks up Swamp Creek from a highway pullout about 3 miles before Rainy Pass. From Snowy Lakes, travel northwest toward Golden Horn's basin to access the north aspect; this is the general basin-access line reported by parties, not pitch-by-pitch beta for the original 1958 North Face route.

bivy.name: Snowy Lakes basin
bivy.notes: This is THE climbers' camp for both Golden Horn and Tower Mountain and the whole point of walking the PCT north. From Rainy Pass it is roughly twenty miles round trip over Cutthroat and Granite Passes, with the trail contouring past Tower Mountain and dropping to about six thousand three hundred feet before a signed spur climbs half a mile of well-graded switchbacks to the lakes. Lower Snowy Lake comes first, Upper is a short way above. From camp, Golden Horn is taken by gullies on its south side, mostly loose class 3 scrambling, ending at a summit block where the last twenty feet of mantling above a big ledge is the one move that stops parties; Tower Mountain's west and south sides are a choice of class 3 gully systems on generally sound rock buried under loose surface debris, while its east face is a sheer wall and no business of a scrambling party. Both can be done from this camp in one long day. August and September are the season; snow on the traverse and the north-facing slopes governs anything earlier.
bivy.water: Both lakes, and they are reliable all season. After the dry crest behind you this is where the water problem ends, which is why parties push through to it rather than stopping short.
bivy.permit: None. This is national forest — no backcountry permit, no quota, nothing to book. Use the established sites rather than making new ones; the meadow here is thin, slow-growing and visibly worn where people have spread out. Campfires are a bad idea on principle at this elevation and are usually banned outright by mid summer under a forest-wide order.
bivy.capacity: A number of established sites at and between the two lakes, mostly one or two tents each, plus more on the meadow benches along the PCT below the turn-off. Popular enough that a summer weekend will see several parties, and heavily so once the larches turn.

bivy.name: Swamp Creek highway pullout, for Mount Hardy's south face
bivy.notes: This is the short way up Mount Hardy and the reason most parties never carry a pack up the PCT for it at all: about four and a half miles and four thousand one hundred feet, done comfortably in a day. Walk west along the highway across Swamp Creek, leave the road and climb north and north-east through timber to gain the prominent ridge on the south side of the peak, then follow the south face, which is largely a walk with occasional easy scrambling on loose talus. It is a different trip entirely from the PCT approach and needs no camp, so it is included here as the honest alternative rather than as a site anyone would choose to sleep at. Parties wanting Hardy together with Golden Horn and Tower should use the PCT and the Snowy Lakes or Methow Pass camps instead; parties wanting Hardy alone should start here.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek itself, immediately below the road, and further water on the lower slopes. None higher on the south face.
bivy.permit: None to stop here. The land is national forest and no camping permit applies. Whether an overnight in a highway pullout is welcome varies, so the uncontroversial answer is to sleep at one of the developed campgrounds east of Washington Pass and drive over in the morning, or to sleep in the Rainy Pass lot.
bivy.capacity: A widened shoulder on SR 20 a couple of miles west of Rainy Pass, just east of Swamp Creek. Room for a few cars. This is a roadside start, not a camp — there are no facilities of any kind.

bivy.name: Methow Pass and the PCT meadow camps below Snowy Lakes
bivy.notes: Methow Pass is where the PCT crosses from the Granite Creek side into the head of the West Fork Methow, and the camps just beyond it are the sheltered alternative to Snowy Lakes for anyone who does not want a night in the open at six thousand seven hundred feet. They cost a little climbing back up on summit morning and are worth it in bad weather. This is also the departure point for Mount Hardy by the long approach: the PCT is left near the pass and a climbers' path leads up toward the peak, which stands directly to the west. Parties combining Hardy with Golden Horn and Tower usually base here or at the lakes and take Hardy on the way out, since the ridge rambling between the lakes and Hardy's south side connects the whole group. Camping on the established sites rather than in fresh meadow matters here more than most places, because the ground is soft and the trail is walked by a steady stream of long-distance hikers all summer.
bivy.water: Good here — this is the drainage side of the crest and the creeks running off toward the West Fork Methow are dependable. It is the reason to choose these camps over the lakes when the wind is up.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping at established sites, no permit and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: A string of established sites in the meadows along the trail around a mile beyond Methow Pass, near where the boot path to the lakes leaves. Enough ground for several parties spread out, and lower and more sheltered than the lake basin.

previousAttempt.reason: Row itself says there is no pitch-level beta for the 1958 North Face; no route-specific source found (web search budget exhausted).

name: Northeast Arête
approach: Same general Snowy Lakes basecamp approach as the standard route (PCT from Rainy Pass), continuing to the base of the northeast side of the peak; expect to find your own way from there.

previousAttempt.reason: No route-specific source found (web search budget exhausted); row only gives the generic Snowy Lakes approach.

name: Gorillas Direct
approach: From the Esmeralda/Lake Ingalls Trailhead at the end of FS-9737, hike the Ingalls Way Trail up switchbacks past several waterfalls. For the Cascadian Couloir and South Headwall, turn right onto the Longs Pass Trail at the junction about 1.7 miles in, climb to Longs Pass (about 6,250 ft) near mile 2.9, and descend the rocky climbers' trail on the far side to Ingalls Creek, cross on a log bridge, and follow the climbers' path up the meadow into the base of the Cascadian Couloir (South Headwall lies further up-basin via the same drainage). For West Ridge, the North Ridge routes, and the West Face Wall (Gorillas in the Mist / Gorillas Direct / King Kong), instead stay on the Ingalls Way Trail over Ingalls Pass (about 6,500 ft, roughly mile 3) and continue past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then follow the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge and contour northwest to Goat Pass (7,600 ft) — the West Face Wall with the Gorillas routes sits in the amphitheater roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, while West Ridge and North Ridge climbers continue over or along Goat Pass toward their respective start points. Camping is common near Goat Pass or down at Ingalls Creek depending on the objective. The North Ridge routes can also be reached from the opposite (Mountaineer Creek) side.
descent: Follow the West Ridge to the summit, or descend the main gully with scrambling/downclimbing, breaking right onto a large bench with a single-rope rappel option before reaching Stuart Pass.

bivy.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.
bivy.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites

bivy.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
bivy.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.
bivy.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
bivy.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Basin Trailhead (North Fork Teanaway Rd)

previousAttempt.reason: No Gorillas Direct source could be opened (web search budget exhausted; guessed URLs 404). Only a Steph Abegg West Ridge page was found, which is a different route. Row dist_km 24.1 / gain 6,150 ft could not be checked.

name: North Slopes via Blum Lakes
approach: Park at the Baker River trailhead at the end of the Baker Lake road (about 800 ft). Walk the Baker River trail for a few minutes to the Blum Creek bridge, then take the faint, flagged climbers' path up the north side of Blum Creek. It is brushy at first, then steep forest to about 4,500 ft; traverse up and south to a talus field near 4,900 ft and cross to Lower Blum Lake, then follow the path to Upper Blum Lake (about 5,020 ft). Travel off the path is very difficult (devil's club, blueberry, brush). North Cascades National Park rules apply: a backcountry permit and camping limits.

previousAttempt.reason: No source could be opened (WTA Blum Lakes page did not return content, guessed countryhighpoints URL 404, and the web search budget was exhausted). Row approach text is detailed but has no gain/distance/timing to build days from.

name: Stonehenge
approach: From a high camp below the Chopping Block above Crescent Creek Basin, the party left at 4 a.m., reached the snow slope below the wall by 5 a.m., then climbed roughly 600 ft of easy rock ramps and ledges to a grassy col at the base of the wall where they racked up.

previousAttempt.notes: The first-ascent party (AAJ) stayed 4 days: approach, another climb, a rest day, then Stonehenge with a 4 am start and 5 am arrival at the snow below the wall. Approach and exit elevations (600 ft trailhead, about 6,400 ft Chopping Block camp) and the 7 h exit come from Abegg's 2008 Southern Pickets report. Day 1's 9 h and 6 mi, day 2's gain (7,880 summit minus 6,400 camp, rounded up), and the miles are estimates; no source gives total distance. The row has no bivy entries.

name: Wild Hair Crack
approach: Via Goodell Creek Trailhead (~600 ft) and the Stump Hollow approach into Crescent Creek Basin (good bivy sites below Mt. Terror), then a narrow gully up to the Himmelhorn-Ottohorn col.
descent: Early season: scramble down; late season: rappel through moats

waypoints.name: Wild Hair Crack start (Himmelhorn-Ottohorn col area)

previousAttempt.notes: Approach elevations and the 7 h exit come from Abegg's Southern Pickets report; route and gully beta come from Mountain Project. The camp elevation in Crescent Creek Basin is not sourced, so day 1 gain uses the about 6,400 ft Chopping Block saddle (from the 600 ft trailhead), and day 2 gain is 7,880 minus about 6,400. Miles and hours on days 1-2 are estimates. The 3-day length matches the first-ascent pattern for Stonehenge (AAJ).

name: Southeast Buttress (South Peak)
approach: From the Lightning Creek trailhead on Ross Lake, the first-ascent party hiked east past Willow Lake, then left the trail to bushwhack through timber and avalanche debris, crossed a ravine, and climbed steep dirt and brush to open timber on the broad shoulder south of the peak. They reached meadows near 5,000 ft and bypassed cliff bands to a saddle at about 6,200 ft below the buttress — roughly six hours from the trailhead — where they bivouacked.

previousAttempt.reason: No second independent source could be opened: the only beta is the first-ascent narrative in the row (Lightning Creek trailhead, bivy at about 6,200 ft) and no timed account of the climb above the bivy, descent or exit was found. Web search budget was exhausted before further sources could be found.

name: East Peak (Northeast Ridge to East Face)
approach: Park at the Esmeralda trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway road and take the Lake Ingalls trail. After about 0.4 mile the Ingalls Way junction bears right, and a second junction near 1.4 miles leads off to Longs Pass; stay on the main trail through Headlight Basin to Ingalls Pass at roughly 3 miles and 6,500 ft, about 2,500 ft of gain. Descend into the basin and traverse to Lake Ingalls, taking the higher trail for the shortest way, or the lower fork if you are camping in Headlight Basin. From the lake, head toward the east side of the peak, keeping to the right of the large couloir there. Easy ledges lead to the base of the northeast ridge.

previousAttempt.notes: Gain is derived from the 4,269 ft trailhead to the 7,480 ft East Peak. Mileage is WTA's 9 mi round trip plus about 1 mile beyond the lake. Hours are an estimate based on Ingalls East Ridge and South Ridge day times (7-13 h). No trip report for this exact route was found. The row gives 2 pitches; Mountain Project describes a 400 ft route of low-5th ridge plus one long face pitch.

name: North Peak Southwest Face
approach: From the Esmeralda Basin Trailhead (FR-9737), follow the old mine road about 0.25 mile to a fork and turn right onto the Ingalls Way trail. Hike roughly 3 miles to Ingalls Pass and on to Ingalls Lake, about 4 miles from the car. Scramble to the notch between the north and south summits, then drop west about 100 feet to a friction slab, where the Southwest Face begins.

previousAttempt.notes: The route description (Class 4 per Beckey via SummitPost; a couple of low-5th moves per the Mountaineers) comes from search snippets, as both sites returned 403. Gain is derived from the 4,269 ft trailhead to the 7,662 ft North Peak; the row has no high point. Miles are WTA's 9 mi round trip to the lake plus about 1 mile to the notch. Lemke's party reached the lake about 9 am after a pre-sunrise start and finished by headlamp. The 9 hours is an estimate.

name: King Kong - Gorillas Direct Direct
approach: From the Esmeralda/Lake Ingalls Trailhead at the end of FS-9737, hike the Ingalls Way Trail up switchbacks past several waterfalls over Ingalls Pass (about 6,500 ft, roughly mile 3), then continue past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, follow the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge, and contour northwest to Goat Pass (7,600 ft). The West Face Wall, home to the Gorillas routes (Gorillas in the Mist / Gorillas Direct / King Kong), sits in the amphitheater roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass. Camping is common near Goat Pass or down at Ingalls Creek.
descent: Follow the West Ridge to the summit, or descend the main W Ridge gully via scrambling/downclimbing, breaking skier's right onto a large bench, single-rope rappel from a fixed anchor, then downclimb to Stuart Pass bivy sites.

bivy.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.
bivy.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites

bivy.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
bivy.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.
bivy.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
bivy.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Basin Trailhead (North Fork Teanaway Rd)

previousAttempt.notes: No timed trip report for King Kong itself could be opened (the FA thread on CascadeClimbers returned 403). Blake's Gorillas in the Mist ascent on the same wall took 2 days car-to-car with a 5 am start and a West Ridge bivy. Day 1 elevations come from the row's waypoints and bivy (4,269 ft trailhead, 6,457 ft Ingalls Pass, about 6,000 ft meadows); its 700 ft loss is approximate. Day 2 gain assumes the wall starts near Goat Pass (7,600 ft per the row) and tops out about 900 ft higher; it is not sourced. Mileage splits the row's 7.2 km (4.5 mi) one-way. Pitch lengths on Mountain Project add up to about 355 m against a listed 273 m.

name: Labor Pains
approach: Shares its start with the Chockstone Route; from there head up and left toward a ledge below a clean slab to begin Labor Pains, which climbs the clean face between the Chockstone Route and The West Face.
descent: Descend via the Chockstone Route's bolted rappel stations back to the base.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, about a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
bivy.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, first come first served

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground
bivy.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
bivy.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee
bivy.capacity: First come first served

bivy.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
bivy.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
bivy.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park
bivy.capacity: Scattered dispersed sites, small parties

previousAttempt.notes: Gain is derived from the row's waypoints (5,200 ft trailhead to 7,760 ft summit = 2,560 ft); the row lists gain_ft 2400. No source gives mileage, so 4 mi round trip is an estimate. Hours are an estimate from NCMG's 1.5 h approach plus a Grade III day. The NCMG page covers the neighbouring West Face (same approach and similar descent with about 6 rappels). The row says 5 pitches; Nicholson describes 4 plus scrambling to the West Face finish.

name: Lover's Lane (couloir)
approach: Begin at the Narada Falls parking area; travel via snowshoe/ski along the (closed, in winter) Reflection Lakes road, then traverse steep hillsides under Denman Peak toward Lane Peak's base, turning sharply uphill at the first steep avalanche funnel to reach the base of the couloir.
descent: From the summit, downclimb or rappel from a tree just below it, then descend moderate slopes to the Lane-Denman saddle and down the steep gully on its far side to rejoin the approach. The 100+ ft rappel into the Zipper is made on the way up, not on the way down.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

bivy.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
bivy.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
bivy.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained in person at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
bivy.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

waypoints.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp

previousAttempt.notes: Gain and miles come from the row (gain_ft 2000; dist_km 3.2 read as one-way, so about 4 mi round trip). Hebert's April 2016 trip on the neighbouring Zipper took about 1 h from the car to the couloir base, 1.25 h up the couloir, and about 4 h car-to-car without summiting. The 6 hours adds time for the summit and the saddle descent and is an estimate. No Lover's Lane-specific trip report could be opened.

name: Freedom or Death
approach: Standard East Face approach; look for the leftward-trending ramp right of Liberty Crack.
descent: Rappel with a 60m rope from the top of P3, or continue up Liberty Crack

previousAttempt.notes: Gain and loss are left at 0 because no source gives the elevation of the east face base and the row has no high point. Approach time and mileage come from the Liberty Crack approach beta; the 6 hours is an estimate. Rappelling from P3 means the route does not reach the summit, but the row has a summit waypoint at 7,720.

name: Freedom Rider
approach: Standard East Face approach; park at the pond pullout near the hairpin turn east of Washington Pass.
descent: Standard Liberty Bell East Face rappel/downclimb via Beckey Gully

previousAttempt.notes: No Freedom Rider trip report with times could be opened (the CascadeClimbers TR returned 403). The 12 hours is extrapolated from Abegg's 10 h car-to-car on neighbouring Liberty Crack, since Mountain Project calls Freedom Rider about 1.5 times the effort of Liberty Crack. Gain is derived from the 5,160 ft hairpin turnout (Kangaroo Temple row) to the 7,720 ft summit. Miles are about 1 mile each way per the east face approach descriptions. Mountain Project lists a 5.11b crux as well as 5.10d, so the row's 5.10d grade understates the route.

name: Sidewinder (Southwest Corner)
approach: Follow the Beckey Gully approach, breaking left at the fork; multiple start options exist depending on the chosen variation, scrambling to a major shelf or ramp below a cave feature.
descent: Standard Liberty Bell descent via the Beckey Route (two rappels)

previousAttempt.notes: Neither source covers Sidewinder itself; the plan relies on the shared Beckey gully approach and descent beta. Gain is derived from the row's elevations (5,380 to 7,720 = 2,340 ft); the row lists gain_ft 2520. Mileage is Outbound's 5 mi round trip. The 8 hours is an estimate, not a reported time.

name: South Face
approach: From Highway 97 south of the Y-junction, drive ~7.5 miles and turn onto Ingalls Creek Road/Trailhead. Hike the Ingalls Creek Trail roughly 8 miles, then leave the trail (right/north) into brushy terrain up Crystal Creek, gaining about 2,200 ft to a base-camp meadow and tarn near 6,000 ft. From the tarn, climb a large talus-apron gully west of the tarn to a col at roughly 7,700-7,880 ft between Little Annapurna and the spires to its south.
descent: Descend the peak's northeast slopes toward Crystal Lake, then follow the outlet stream back down to the Crystal Creek base camp.

previousAttempt.reason: The only detailed beta is on SummitPost (route page and trip report), which returns 403. Lemke's page has no approach or timing figures, so there are not two usable sources. Search snippets agree with the row: about 8 mi up Ingalls Creek, a 6-7 h approach to a tarn camp in Crystal Creek, and a descent past Crystal Lake.

name: North Ridge
approach: Shares the same general approach drainage as the West Route (Jug Creek/Bluff Lake/Cliff Lake benches) to gain the west side of the mountain, then continues around/up to the base of the north ridge rather than the west-ridge saddle system.
descent: Typically descended via the West Route rather than reversing the North Ridge.

previousAttempt.reason: The Chaval beta is on SummitPost and CascadeClimbers, and both return 403. No source I could open describes the North Ridge.

name: Northeast Ridge
approach: Reached only by first climbing Mount Crowder by its Southwest Route, from the col between Phantom Peak and Crowder, and continuing down the far side; there is no separate trailhead approach to this ridge on its own.
descent: This IS the descent line; it drops from Crowder's summit to Pickell Pass.

bivy.name: Pickell Pass
bivy.notes: Open camp at the pass at the foot of the ridge, used by traverse parties who climb Crowder by its Southwest Route and descend this ridge to the pass.
bivy.water: Snowmelt
bivy.permit: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone)
bivy.capacity: A few tents

previousAttempt.reason: This ridge is only done as the descent leg of multi-day Picket traverses. Steph Abegg (Mystery Ridge Enchainment, 7 days, about 55 mi) and Mount Baker Experience describe it as grassy Class 3 ledges with one or two 5th-class downclimbs or brushy rappels, ending at a heather-bench camp at Pickell Pass. Neither gives route-level timing, so a stand-alone plan would invent figures. Abegg's Day 4 (Pioneer, Crowder, Pickell Pass: +4,480 / -4,050 ft, 5.8 mi) is the best template.
